edition.sessionCovered: Tue, Nov 10 (Brent slides to $91.83 as Iran deal proposal reaches Trump · CPI 8:30 AM ET · BTC $74,089 · Gold $4,095)
edition.stripNote: Tue 10 Nov. Brent slides to $91.83 after crashing 5.85% on Monday — its steepest weekly loss since the pandemic — as Qatar's PM delivers Iran's $8 billion Hormuz deal proposal to Trump. Key cabinet members oppose the terms. WTI at $85.93. October CPI due at 8:30 AM ET — the BLS will not publish 12-month changes because October 2025 was not collected during last year's government shutdown, making the monthly readings (consensus +0.2% MoM) the key figure. Gold at $4,095 as lower oil tempers inflation fears. BTC holds at $74,089 ahead of CPI.

overview: Oil dominated Tuesday's pre-CPI session after Brent crude crashed 5.85% on Monday to settle at $92.57 per barrel — its steepest weekly decline since the start of the Covid-19 pandemic. Brent continued lower in Asian trading toward $91.83, down 0.8% on the day. The catalyst was twofold: President Trump told CNN that fresh Iran strikes are 'highly unlikely' while talks progress, and Qatar's prime minister delivered an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz to the White House. Iran has reportedly signed off on terms that would halt attacks on Gulf tankers and reopen the strait in exchange for the US lifting its naval blockade and releasing $8 billion in frozen Iranian funds. Key cabinet members — Treasury Secretary Bessent, Commerce Secretary Lutnick, Secretary of State Rubio and Secretary of War Hegseth — reportedly oppose, with Rubio calling the demands 'outrageous and ridiculous.' WTI fell to $85.93. A Reuters survey shows OPEC output rose 1.38 million bpd in October to 22.87 million bpd, and JPMorgan estimates a global surplus of 1.4 million bpd. Morgan Stanley notes that Dated Brent has slipped to a discount to nearby futures — a sign of weakening physical demand. The October CPI report is due at 8:30 AM ET, though the BLS will not publish 12-month headline changes because October 2025 data was not collected during last year's government shutdown. Monthly consensus sits at 0.2%, down from September's 0.6%.

Gold traded near $4,095 per ounce, rising 0.7% on Tuesday morning as oil's collapse tempered inflation fears and the dollar softened following Democrats' sweeping midterm victory. The midterms dealt Trump a significant political setback, with voters citing cost of living and the Iran war; markets now expect two years of legislative gridlock, though Trump retains executive power over trade and foreign policy. Silver firmed to $52.51. Bitcoin remained under pressure at $74,089, with spot ETF outflows totalling $1.28 billion for the week and the Fear and Greed Index sitting at 34 (Fear). Ethereum at $2,107, still underperforming BTC. The S&P 500 rallied 2.35% on Monday to 7,550 as the oil crash eased inflation concerns — the Dow surged 1,100 points. Copper steadied near $6.29 per pound ($13,855/t LME) as the weaker dollar offset risk-off sentiment. Newcastle coal slipped toward $141 per tonne. LME zinc closed at $3,744, tin at $46,200, and nickel at $16,400. China's November 27 deadline to re-impose export controls on gallium, germanium, antimony and superhard materials is now 17 days away. USDA crop estimates are due later today, with analysts expecting a higher US soybean harvest forecast and lower US corn crop estimate.

watchItems.title: October CPI at 8:30 AM ET: a unique release with no annual rate
watchItems.text: The October CPI report is due Tuesday morning but will be unusually limited: the BLS will not publish 12-month headline or core inflation changes because October 2025 data was not collected during last year's government shutdown. Monthly consensus is 0.2% MoM (down from September's 0.6%), with core at 0.2%. The Cleveland Fed nowcast points to 3.7% annual if the figure were calculated. A soft monthly print could ease the 81% probability of a December rate hike and support risk assets; a hot reading would reinforce hawkish expectations and could push gold below $4,000 support. The monthly figure becomes the market's proxy for the annual rate, amplifying its importance.

watchItems.title: Iran's $8 billion Hormuz deal proposal: cabinet opposes, attacks continue
watchItems.text: Qatar's PM delivered an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz to the White House on Monday. Iran has reportedly signed off on terms: halt attacks on tankers and reopen the strait in exchange for the US lifting its naval and economic blockade and releasing $8 billion in frozen funds. Iran dropped its demand to charge transit fees but still refuses to put its nuclear programme on the table. Key cabinet members — Bessent, Lutnick, Rubio, Hegseth — oppose. Rubio called the demands 'outrageous and ridiculous.' A similar memorandum in May collapsed after Iranian tanker attacks. Despite diplomatic hints, four attacks in the strait occurred November 1–3 and the Houthis claimed a strike on Saudi Aramco's Riyadh offices. Brent's 16% weekly crash shows the market pricing peace — any breakdown would trigger a violent snap-back in oil.

watchItems.title: China's Nov 27 export-control deadline: 17 days and counting
watchItems.text: China's suspension of its prohibition on gallium, germanium, antimony and superhard material exports to the US expires November 27 — now just 17 days away. The suspension, announced November 9, 2025 as part of the Busan truce, has not restored meaningful export volumes. Gallium remains near $2,100/kg (up 130%+ since early 2025). Overseas tungsten APT holds above $3,300/mtu, nearly quadruple Chinese domestic levels. The Democrats' midterm sweep introduces political uncertainty: a divided Congress could slow any bilateral agreement to extend the suspension. Re-imposition would hit semiconductors, ammunition, hardened steel and EV battery supply chains.

watchItems.title: Oil's 16% weekly crash: structural shift or snapback risk?
watchItems.text: Brent has fallen 16% in a week — its steepest decline since the pandemic — on a combination of Iran deal hopes, rising OPEC output (+1.38M bpd in October), and a JPMorgan-estimated 1.4M bpd surplus. Morgan Stanley notes Dated Brent has slipped to a discount to futures, signalling weakening physical demand. The US SPR fell to 279.5 million barrels, its lowest since October 1982. Iraq reached understandings with the US to allow oil exports through Hormuz via a lane near Oman. However, Eurasia Group still pegs peace odds at just 10%, and the IRGC continues to attack shipping. Murban crude rose 3.4% to $99.17 in Asian trading — tight physical Gulf supply suggests the collapse may be overshoot.

desk.name: Gold
desk.m: Pulled back from Mon's $4,141 intraday high · oil crash tempers inflation bid · midterm-driven dollar weakness supports
desk.sum: Gold traded near $4,095 per ounce on Tuesday morning, rising 0.7% as oil's crash tempered inflation fears and the dollar softened after Democrats' midterm sweep. Gold touched approximately $4,141 intraday on Monday — its highest since early October — before retreating as the oil collapse reduced inflation-hedge demand. The weaker dollar, lower bond yields, and continued Hormuz uncertainty provide a floor. Central bank buying continues at elevated levels. October CPI at 8:30 AM ET is the key near-term catalyst — a soft monthly print could extend gains toward Goldman's $4,150 target, while a hot reading could push gold back toward $4,000.

desk.name: Silver
desk.m: Tracking gold's recovery · gold-silver ratio ~78 · industrial demand from solar intact
desk.sum: Silver firmed to $52.51 per ounce, rising 1.2% on Tuesday as it tracked gold's recovery amid lower oil prices and dollar weakness. The gold-silver ratio sits near 78. Silver's dual role as a precious and industrial metal continues to provide leverage: the oil crash helps the precious bid through lower inflation expectations, while solar panel manufacturing demand underpins the industrial side. The CPI report and USDA crop data today are the key catalysts.

desk.name: Oil
desk.m: WTI $85.93 · Brent crashed 5.85% Mon to $92.57 · 16% weekly decline · Qatar delivers Iran $8B deal · OPEC output +1.38M bpd Oct
desk.sum: Brent continued lower toward $91.83 per barrel on Tuesday, down 0.8%, after crashing 5.85% on Monday to settle at $92.57 — its steepest weekly decline since the pandemic at 16%. WTI fell to $85.93. Qatar's PM delivered Iran's proposal to reopen Hormuz in exchange for $8 billion in frozen funds, though key cabinet members oppose. OPEC output rose 1.38 million bpd in October; JPMorgan estimates a 1.4 million bpd global surplus. Morgan Stanley notes Dated Brent has slipped to a discount to futures. The US SPR fell to 279.5 million barrels, its lowest since October 1982. Iraq reached understandings with the US to export oil through Hormuz via a lane near Oman.

desk.name: Copper
desk.m: LME $13,855/t · dollar weakness post-midterms supports · lower tariff risk under gridlock · Chile output still tight
desk.sum: Copper edged up to approximately $6.29 per pound ($13,855 per tonne LME 3M), supported by dollar weakness after the midterm results. Democrats' sweep reduces the likelihood of new US refined copper tariffs — Saxo notes this could move US-held inventories back into global markets, easing tight Chinese premiums. Chilean supply remains constrained. SMM reports Chinese copper stocks at approximately 60,000 mt, roughly 140,000 mt below the same period last year. The oil crash has mixed implications: lower energy costs help smelters, but risk-off sentiment weighs on industrial metals broadly.

desk.name: Coal
desk.m: Down from $152 Oct high · oil crash eases energy complex · LNG tightness still provides floor
desk.sum: Newcastle coal slipped toward $141 per tonne, retreating from the $152 October high reached on October 30. Oil's 16% weekly crash has eased the broader energy complex, but coal retains support from continued LNG tightness — QatarEnergy's force majeure extends through year-end. If the Iran deal materialises and Hormuz reopens, both coal and LNG prices could face significant downside as energy supply normalises. The coal-to-gas switching dynamic remains a key price anchor in Asia.

desk.name: Platinum
desk.m: Up ~8% over 2 weeks · WPIC supply deficit · hydrogen economy demand
desk.sum: Platinum rose 0.8% to approximately $1,546 per ounce, continuing to benefit from both precious-metals safe-haven demand and industrial fundamentals. The WPIC supply deficit narrative and hydrogen electrolysis growth continue to attract buying. Platinum's outperformance relative to palladium reflects the market's preference for metals with diversified demand drivers. Oil's crash reduces energy costs for platinum miners but also tempers the inflation-hedge bid.

desk.name: Palladium
desk.m: Held above $1,000 support · EV transition still a headwind · Nornickel plant maintenance
desk.sum: Palladium rose 0.9% to approximately $1,033 per ounce, holding above the $1,000 psychological support level. The metal remains vulnerable to the EV transition narrative — battery EVs require no catalytic converter. However, Nornickel's plant overhaul and firm global ICE vehicle demand provide near-term support. The broader precious metals bid, driven by dollar weakness and lower oil, lifted palladium alongside gold and silver.

desk.name: Hormuz Terminal
desk.m: Iran signs off on Qatar-brokered deal · $8B for Hormuz reopening · Cabinet opposes · attacks continue · Iraq lane via Oman
desk.sum: The Strait of Hormuz risk level remains critical despite significant diplomatic movement. Qatar's PM delivered an Iranian proposal to the White House on Monday: Iran would reopen the strait and halt attacks in exchange for the US lifting its blockade and releasing $8 billion in frozen funds. Iran has reportedly signed off, dropping its demand for transit fees but keeping its nuclear programme off the table. Key cabinet members oppose — Rubio called the demands 'outrageous and ridiculous.' Despite the diplomatic track, four attacks occurred between November 1 and 3, with traffic through the strait 'substantially reduced' to single-digit to low-double-digit transits per day. The Houthis claimed a strike on Saudi Aramco's Riyadh offices. Iraq reached understandings with the US to allow oil exports via a lane near Oman. Eurasia Group still pegs peace odds at just 10%.
desk.src: OilPrice.com · Reuters · Gulf News · Seatrade Maritime

desk.name: Corn
desk.m: USDA estimates due today · analysts expect lower US crop estimate · managed money net short
desk.sum: December corn edged up 0.2% to approximately 443¢ per bushel, supported by positioning ahead of the USDA's crop estimates due later today. Analysts polled by Reuters expect the USDA to lower its US corn crop estimate, which could lift prices. Managed money remains net short. Corn has lost about 8% over the past month. The October CPI and USDA reports are the twin macro catalysts for agricultural markets today.

desk.name: Wheat
desk.m: Down ~16% m/m · Abu Dhabi talks could restart Black Sea grain shipments · Russian exports at half normal
desk.sum: December wheat slipped 0.5% to approximately 588¢ per bushel. Prices fell on hopes that talks in Abu Dhabi could restart stalled Russian and Ukrainian Black Sea grain shipments. StoneX's Matt Ammermann noted Russian wheat exports are running at about half their normal volume, so a deal could significantly boost global supply. Wheat has shed about 16% over the past month. The USDA's crop estimates today will provide updated supply-demand projections.

desk.name: Soybean
desk.m: USDA to raise US harvest forecast · Chinese buying muted · Goldman sees comfortable balance
desk.sum: Soybeans edged up 0.1% to approximately 1,195¢ per bushel, supported by positioning ahead of the USDA's crop estimates. Analysts expect the USDA to raise its US soybean harvest forecast. The global soybean balance remains comfortable per Goldman Sachs. Chinese buying interest is muted as demand concerns persist. The strong dollar, although weakening post-midterms, continues to weigh on US export competitiveness.

desk.name: Cryptocurrencies
desk.m: ETH $2,107 · spot ETF outflows $1.28B weekly · Fear & Greed at 34 · midterms add regulatory uncertainty
desk.sum: Bitcoin slipped to $74,089, extending its decline as risk appetite remained fragile despite US equities rallying strongly on Monday. Spot Bitcoin ETF outflows totalled approximately $1.28 billion for the week — the steepest since June. Democrats' midterm sweep has raised regulatory uncertainty: a divided Congress could stall the crypto-friendly legislation Trump had championed. Ethereum dropped to $2,107, still underperforming BTC with the ETH/BTC ratio near multi-week lows. The Fear and Greed Index sits at 34 (Fear). Leveraged liquidations exceeded $1 billion in 24 hours. October CPI at 8:30 AM ET is the key macro catalyst — a soft print could trigger a relief rally.

desk.name: LNG
desk.m: JKM low-$34s · TTF $34 · HH $3.02 · QatarEnergy force majeure extends · oil crash raises deal risk for LNG
desk.sum: Asian LNG spot (JKM) holds in the low-$34 range per MMBtu for December delivery. QatarEnergy's force majeure extends through at least end-December 2026, keeping about 5 bcm of supply offline. EU storage sits at 74.7%, roughly 17% below the five-year average ahead of winter. Henry Hub firmed to $3.02. Oil's dramatic crash — and the Qatari-brokered Iran deal proposal — raise the possibility that Hormuz could reopen, which would be a significant bearish catalyst for LNG as Qatari cargoes resume. Until then, the approaching Northern Hemisphere winter supports prices.
desk.src: S&P Global · Global LNG Hub · OilPrice.com

desk.name: Sulfur
desk.m: FOB Kuwait $765 · Iran deal proposal could unlock supply · Nov 27 export-control deadline
desk.sum: Sulfur remains elevated at approximately $1,200 per tonne CFR Southeast Asia. The Iran deal proposal is a potential game-changer for sulfur: if Hormuz reopens, Middle Eastern sulfur shipments could resume, easing the acute supply squeeze that has driven prices higher. FOB Kuwait holds near $765 (KPC). However, with cabinet opposition to the deal and continued IRGC attacks, relief is not imminent. Chinese domestic sulfur holds near 7,200 yuan per tonne. The November 27 export-control deadline adds further uncertainty.

desk.name: Potash
desk.m: BPC India $383 CFR · China benchmark ~$348 · demand firm for 2026
desk.sum: Muriate of potash (MOP) CFR Brazil holds near $367 per tonne, largely unchanged. BPC's India contract remains approximately $35 above China's 2026 benchmark at $383 per tonne CFR. Argus Media forecasts potash demand to remain firm through 2026. Belarus and Russia still account for about 40% of global supply despite Western sanctions. Oil's crash has limited direct impact on potash, though lower energy costs could reduce production expenses.

desk.name: Antimony
desk.m: 17 days to Nov 27 deadline · Document No. 46 suspension expiring · market flat after Oct pullback from ¥100k+
desk.sum: Chinese antimony (#1 ingot) holds near 93,500 yuan per tonne, flat after an October pullback from the August high above 100,000 yuan. The critical near-term catalyst is the November 27 deadline — now just 17 days away — when the suspension of China's export prohibition on antimony, gallium, germanium and superhard materials expires. Democrats' midterm sweep introduces political uncertainty around any bilateral extension. Re-imposition would tighten supply for ammunition, flame retardants and semiconductor manufacturing.

desk.name: Gallium & Germanium
desk.m: Up >130% since early 2025 · 17 days to Nov 27 deadline · China 98% of supply · midterms complicate extension
desk.sum: Gallium holds near $2,100 per kilogram outside China, up over 130% since early 2025. The November 27 deadline is now just 17 days away. The Democrats' midterm victory — and the resulting political gridlock — could complicate any bilateral agreement to extend the Busan truce suspension. China produces about 98% of global gallium. Western supply-chain development is advancing but timelines stretch beyond 2027. The semiconductor downturn adds demand uncertainty, but the strategic premium remains elevated.

desk.name: Vanadium
desk.m: Soft on weak steel demand · VRFB adoption timeline uncertain · China-Russia-SA control 90%+ supply
desk.sum: Vanadium pentoxide (V₂O₅) holds near $5.02 per pound, soft as steel demand weakens amid the global risk-off environment. Oil's crash reduces energy input costs for steelmakers but also signals broader demand uncertainty. The long-term bull case rests on vanadium redox flow batteries (VRFBs) for grid-scale energy storage, but large-scale adoption timing remains uncertain. China, Russia and South Africa control over 90% of supply.

desk.name: Cocoa
desk.m: Hit 4-month low below $5,100 on Nov 6 · ICE inventories at 2.5-yr high · mid-crop could fall 42–50%
desk.sum: ICE cocoa trades near $5,050 per tonne, at a four-month low after falling below $5,100 on November 6. Rising ICE warehouse inventories — now at a 2.5-year high of 3,740,476 bags — continue to pressure prices. Irregular October rainfall in Ivory Coast, linked to El Niño, threatens flowering. Reuters projects the 2026/27 mid-crop could fall 42–50% to 300,000–350,000 tonnes. Traders also fear Harmattan winds in December–January. StoneX projects 2026/27 global output could fall 9.6%, potentially turning the current surplus into a deficit.

desk.name: Cobalt
desk.m: DRC quotas 96,600 t/yr · Asian market remains pressured in Q4 · NMC-to-LFP shift continues
desk.sum: Cobalt holds at approximately $33,525 per tonne, under pressure. S&P Global reports the Asian cobalt market is expected to remain pressured in Q4 amid lackluster demand. The DRC (70% of global mine supply) maintains export quotas of 96,600 tonnes per year through 2027. The EV battery chemistry shift from NMC to LFP continues to structurally reduce cobalt intensity. CME notes that cobalt and lithium face structural shifts since the last cycle top.

desk.name: Lithium
desk.m: Fell below ¥95k — lowest in nearly a year · Nov production to rise 35% MoM · supply overwhelms demand
desk.sum: Chinese lithium carbonate futures fell below 95,000 yuan per tonne in November, the lowest in nearly a year, and trade near ¥92,000. Mysteel projects Chinese lithium carbonate production will rise 35% month-on-month in November as spodumene-based output expands — a significant bearish signal. The EU's plan to cap Chinese EV imports at 350,000 units per year adds a demand headwind. Downstream buyers remain cautious, purchasing mainly for rigid needs. Goldman Sachs projects a 444,000-tonne global surplus by 2028.

desk.name: Rubber
desk.m: $2.55/kg · SE Asia supply tight · fungal blight ongoing · auto demand solid
desk.sum: Natural rubber (RSS3) trades near $2,550 per tonne ($2.55/kg), in a range-bound pattern. Southeast Asian supply remains tight with Thailand, Indonesia and Malaysia — producing 70% of global latex — still affected by Pestalotiopsis fungal leaf blight. Auto-sector demand remains solid despite the tech-sector turmoil, supported by replacement-tyre cycles. Oil's crash reduces synthetic rubber production costs, which could cap natural rubber upside.

desk.name: Uranium
desk.m: Spot mid-$80s · long-term contracts near $96–99/lb — approaching $100 · AI-driven demand · Kazakhstan shortfalls
desk.sum: Uranium spot holds near $86 per pound U₃O₈, stabilised in the mid-$80s. Long-term contract prices continue to rise, with Crux Investor reporting record US contract prices near $99 per pound — close to the $100 milestone — as utilities lock in supply amid energy security concerns. Over 440 reactors operate worldwide with 60+ under construction. AI data-centre power demand remains a structural driver. Kazakhstan (43% of mine output) faces production shortfalls from acid supply constraints. The Sprott Physical Uranium Trust continues to absorb spot supply.

desk.name: Rare Earths
desk.m: CREA November index fell to 254.7 · ex-China FOB $109–121/kg · Lynas shutdown adds supply risk
desk.sum: Neodymium-praseodymium (NdPr) oxide trades near $72 per kilogram domestically in China, while ex-China FOB prices sit at $109–121/kg per SMM. The China Rare Earth Industry Association's November index fell to 254.7, extending October's weakness. Lynas' Malaysian plant is undergoing a one-month maintenance shutdown and its Kalgoorlie plant is halting for power grid upgrades, putting December-quarter ex-China output under pressure. Heavy rare earths (dysprosium, terbium) remain elevated in Western markets, with Rotterdam in-bond terbium at $7,300–8,300/kg.

desk.name: Manganese
desk.m: South Africa 37% · Gabon 18% · CIF China flat · steel demand stable
desk.sum: Manganese ore (44% Mn content) trades near $4.40 per dry metric tonne unit CIF China, with minor fluctuations. South Africa supplies about 37% of global ore and Gabon 18%. Steel production consumes 90% of manganese demand. Oil's crash could modestly reduce steel producers' energy costs. High-purity manganese sulfate for EV batteries is an emerging demand driver, though the lithium carbonate price decline reduces the urgency of battery chemistry diversification.

desk.name: Nickel
desk.m: Flat · Indonesia 67% mine · surplus persists · Coface: nickel has a future despite low prices
desk.sum: LME nickel holds near $16,400 per tonne (3M), essentially flat. Nickel's surplus persists as Indonesian NPI and HPAL expansions continue. Coface notes that nickel 'has a future despite low prices,' citing growing battery demand. The weaker dollar post-midterms provides modest support. Chinese smelter maintenance provides short-term tightness. Oil's crash reduces nickel pig iron production costs in Indonesia, potentially adding to the surplus overhang.

desk.name: Tin
desk.m: Down from $48,225 on Nov 3 · LME stocks near 4,000 mt · Myanmar ban still constraining supply
desk.sum: LME tin trades near $46,200 per tonne, consolidating after declining from $48,225 on November 3. SMM expects the market to trade in a $47,500–51,000 range. LME inventory holds near 4,000 mt — low for the year — providing a floor, though SMM notes this support has weakened. Structural supply constraints persist from Myanmar's Wa State mining ban and Indonesian export licensing tightness. Oil's crash and the broader risk-off mood have overshadowed the tight fundamental picture.

desk.name: Zinc
desk.m: Consolidating at lows · TCs deeply negative · LME stocks down 64% YTD to 146,375 mt · smelter cuts continue
desk.sum: LME zinc closed at $3,744 per tonne, up 0.69% as the market consolidated at low levels. SMM notes zinc is 'digesting employment data' and expects consolidation in the short term. Treatment charges remain deeply negative. LME inventories fell to 146,375 mt as of November 9 — down approximately 64% year-to-date. Several Chinese and European smelters have cut output. The fundamental picture remains tight despite the broader risk-off environment weighing on base metals.

desk.name: Tungsten
desk.m: Overseas APT $3,300+ · China domestic APT ¥550k/t Nov · Chongyi raises Nov contract prices · Western prices 3–4x China
desk.sum: Overseas APT holds above $3,300 per mtu, with Western prices running roughly three to four times Chinese domestic levels. Chongyi tungsten enterprises raised long-term contract prices for the first half of November. Domestic APT remains at 550,000 yuan per tonne. Fastmarkets reports the tungsten market is 'fragmenting' as Chinese domestic prices decouple from export prices. China's export controls on tungsten processing technology have created a severe non-Chinese supply crisis. The November 27 Busan truce deadline remains a critical uncertainty.

desk.name: Helium
desk.m: Up 358% YTD · Ras Laffan repair 3–5 years · Iran deal could accelerate repair timeline
desk.sum: Grade-A helium trades near $390 per thousand cubic feet, at critical levels. The Iran deal proposal introduces a potential catalyst: if Hormuz reopens and the broader conflict de-escalates, repair work on Qatar's Ras Laffan facilities — currently estimated at 3–5 years — could potentially accelerate. Qatar and the US together supply about 81% of global helium. Russia's export controls extend through 2027. Commercial inventories remain at their lowest since 2008. Semiconductor fabs, MRI machines and space launch consume most demand.

desk.name: Phosphate
desk.m: OCP 30% global · DAP $560/t · sulfur cost surge pressuring economics · Iran deal could ease sulfur costs
desk.sum: Phosphate rock trades near $120 per tonne FOB Morocco, with Morocco's OCP Group controlling about 30% of global trade. DAP prices sit near $560 per tonne CFR India. The sulfur price surge continues to pressure phosphate production economics, as sulfur is a key input for phosphoric acid. If the Iran deal materialises and Middle Eastern sulfur supply resumes, phosphate producers could see significant cost relief. China periodically restricts fertiliser exports to protect domestic supply.
